stages.title: Advanced linguistics and grammar
stages.hook: Why can Spanish say "Llueve" with no subject, and "Me gusta el cine" with the thing liked as subject? Linguistics explains the patterns.
explain: Linguistics studies language on several levels: phonetics and phonology (sounds), morphology (word structure), syntax (sentence structure), semantics (meaning) and pragmatics (use in context). Spanish is a pro-drop language: rich verb morphology allows null subjects ("Hablo español"). It has verb-initial and flexible word order, with the order shaped by information structure: "Llegó Juan" presents Juan as new information.

Verbs such as gustar are experiencer-subject structures: in "Me gusta el cine" the grammatical subject is "el cine", and "me" is an indirect object. Aspect (preterite and imperfect), mood (indicative, subjunctive) and the clitic system ("se lo di") are central. Differential object marking uses "a" before specific human objects: "Veo a Ana".
stages.mnemonic: Gustar: the thing pleases me; I am not the subject.
items: mood used for unreal or uncertain

gq.q: In "Me gustan los libros", what is the grammatical subject?
gq.why: The verb agrees with los libros, which is the subject.

o: I said it to myself quietly
gq.why: Se replaces le before lo, and the clitics precede the verb.

panel.q: Why is Spanish called a pro-drop language?
o: Subject pronouns can be omitted because verb endings identify the person
panel.why: Rich verbal inflection makes explicit subjects optional.

panel.q: Why is "Veo a Ana" but "Veo la casa"?
o: Specific human direct objects take personal a
Ana is feminine, so the verb needs an extra a before it
panel.why: Differential object marking applies to specific, animate, usually human objects.

panel.q: What is the difference between pragmatics and semantics?
panel.model: Semantics deals with literal meaning of words and sentences; pragmatics with meaning in context, such as what the speaker intends.
panel.why: Levels of meaning.

teach.model: Linguists study sounds, word structure, sentences, meaning and use. Spanish lets speakers omit the subject because verb endings show the person. Verbs like gustar work differently from English like.

stages.title: Historical development of the language
stages.hook: Latin "terra" and "porta" became "tierra" and "puerta". How did a language change itself?
explain: Spanish developed from the Vulgar Latin spoken in the Iberian Peninsula after Roman conquest. The earliest written Spanish traces are the Glosas Emilianenses (around the 10th-11th century), and the epic "Cantar de mio Cid" survives from about 1200. Castilian became prestigious as Castile expanded during the Reconquista. Antonio de Nebrija published the first grammar of Spanish in 1492, and the Real Academia Española was founded in 1713.

Sound changes include diphthongisation of stressed short e and o (terra to tierra, porta to puerta), initial f becoming h (farina to harina, now silent), and palatalisation (annum to año). Arabic contributed thousands of words (aceite, almohada), and later indigenous American languages added words such as chocolate, tomate and canoa. Standardisation and spelling reform continue today.
stages.mnemonic: Latín → latín vulgar → castellano: terra, tierra.
items: sound change from f to h
a word borrowed from another language
sentences: Nebrija wrote the first grammar in 1492.

gq.why: Stressed short o became ue: porta to puerta.

gq.q: When did Nebrija publish the first Spanish grammar?
gq.why: The Gramática de la lengua castellana appeared in 1492.

panel.q: Why is the h in "harina" silent?
o: It comes from Latin f, which became h and was later lost
It was never written in old Spanish and was added much later
It is a borrowed Arabic letter
panel.why: Latin farina gave Spanish harina; the aspirated h disappeared from pronunciation.

panel.q: Why did Castilian become the basis of standard Spanish?
panel.model: The political and cultural power of the Kingdom of Castile spread its variety, which was then codified by grammarians and the Academy.
panel.why: Standardisation follows power.

panel.q: The change of Latin annum to Spanish año is an example of...
panel.why: Latin nn became the palatal nasal ñ.

teach.model: Spanish grew out of Vulgar Latin in Iberia. Sound changes like terra to tierra made it different from Latin. Castile gave it its standard form, Nebrija wrote its first grammar and the Academy was founded later. Arabic and native American languages added words.

stages.title: Literature and cultural discourse
stages.hook: Why do people say Latin American literature changed the world in the 1960s?
explain: Hispanic literature joins a long cultural conversation. Key works include "Don Quijote" (Cervantes), the Golden Age theatre of Lope de Vega and Calderón, and the poetry of Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz. The 20th-century "Boom" brought García Márquez, Vargas Llosa, Cortázar and Fuentes to a worldwide audience, with experimental structure and magical realism. Other major voices are Borges, Neruda, Mistral, Rosario Castellanos, Elena Poniatowska and many contemporary writers.

Cultural discourse asks who tells the story and who is silenced. Critical lenses include postcolonial, feminist, historical and reader-response. Intertextuality links texts: Borges rewrites and comments on earlier works. Discourse analysis studies how language shapes ideas in media and politics. Interpretations must be supported by close reading of the text.
stages.mnemonic: Un texto habla con otros textos.
items: a text referring to another text
a narrative technique mixing real and fantastic
sentences: The Boom made the region famous.
The critic reads the text closely.

gq.q: Which writer is associated with the Latin American Boom?
gq.why: Cortázar was a leading Boom author.

o: The relationship between texts that echo one another
Spelling variation across different regions and times
gq.why: A text may allude to, quote or rewrite another.

panel.q: Why is the literary canon debated?
o: Choices of what counts as important can exclude voices
panel.why: Selection reflects history and power, so critics ask whose voices are missing.

panel.q: How can two critics read the same novel differently?
panel.model: Each critic uses a different lens, such as feminist or postcolonial, and supports the reading with evidence from the text.
panel.why: Plural interpretation.

panel.q: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz is associated with...
panel.why: She was a Mexican nun, poet and scholar of the seventeenth century.

teach.model: Spanish-language literature has many voices from Spain and the Americas. Critics use different lenses to read a work. They ask whose voices are heard, and they support their ideas with evidence from the text.

points.ask: How do I support my reading?

stages.title: Advanced academic writing
stages.hook: What is the difference between "esto demuestra que" and "esto sugiere que"? Academic Spanish measures its claims.
explain: Advanced academic writing in Spanish builds an argument with a clear thesis. A typical article has a resumen, introducción, marco teórico, metodología, resultados, discusión and conclusiones. The introduction identifies a gap in the literature and states the objective: "El presente trabajo tiene como objetivo analizar...".

Stance is controlled with hedges ("podría", "parece", "tiende a") and boosters ("sin duda", "claramente"). Use nominalisation, the pasiva refleja and impersonal "se" for objectivity. Cohesion: "no obstante", "asimismo", "por lo tanto", "en este sentido". Cite consistently (APA, Chicago) and avoid plagiarism. Maintain correct agreement, tenses and accents in long sentences.
sentences: This study aims to analyse the data.
The results could suggest a trend.

o: Los resultados parecen indicar una relación.
Los resultados prueban todo, sin ninguna duda posible.
gq.why: Parecen indicar matches the strength of the evidence.

gq.q: What does the introduction of an article do?
o: Presents the objective and the gap in knowledge
Gives only the results and the final conclusion of it
gq.why: It places the study in the field and states the aim.

panel.q: Why is the impersonal "se" common in academic Spanish?
o: It focuses on the action and sounds objective
panel.why: Not naming the doer maintains an objective tone.

panel.q: Why should claims be proportionate to evidence?
panel.model: Claims that go beyond the evidence are not credible, so academic writers use hedges to be accurate and honest.
panel.why: Epistemic caution.

panel.q: Which connector adds a further point?
panel.why: Asimismo means likewise or also.

teach.model: A research article has an abstract, introduction, theory, method, results, discussion and conclusion. State your aim clearly. Use cautious words and connectors, and cite your sources.

stages.title: Professional translation
stages.hook: A contract says "El arrendatario deberá abonar la renta". How would a translator render this faithfully and clearly?
explain: Professional translation covers legal, medical, technical and literary texts. Each field has terminology and conventions: legal Spanish uses the future of obligation ("deberá abonar") and formulaic phrases; English prefers "shall" or "must" depending on the style guide. Translators use glossaries, translation memory tools and style guides, and revise their work. Machine translation can speed a first draft but requires post-editing.

Ethics include accuracy, confidentiality and honesty about the limits of one's expertise. Certified translations ("traducción jurada") are signed by authorised translators in Spain. Localisation adapts dates (dd/mm/aaaa), units, currency and cultural references. Choose a variety of target Spanish (Spain or Latin America) consistently, for instance "ordenador" or "computadora".
sentences: The tenant must pay the rent.
We use a glossary for consistency.

o: Dates, units, currency and cultural references
gq.why: It adapts the text to the target market.

panel.q: Why should a translator use the same term for the same concept throughout?
o: It prevents confusion and keeps the meaning precise
panel.why: Consistency matters especially in legal and technical texts.

panel.q: Why must a translator keep texts confidential?
panel.model: Documents often contain sensitive information, and clients must be able to trust that it will not be shared.
panel.why: Professional ethics.

panel.q: A text for Mexico uses "computadora". For Spain you would probably choose...
panel.why: Ordenador is the usual word in Spain.

teach.model: Professional translators specialise in fields like law or medicine. They use glossaries and style guides to keep terms consistent, check their work, and keep documents private. Machine translation needs human checking.

stages.title: Interpretation of complex communication
stages.hook: A diplomat says "Lo estudiaremos con atención". Is that yes, no, or maybe? How does an interpreter decide?
explain: Complex communication contains more than words: implicature, politeness, irony, cultural references and silence. Grice's maxims (quantity, quality, relation, manner) explain how speakers imply meaning by flouting them. In many contexts "Lo pensaré" or "Ya veremos" can be a polite refusal.

Interpreters analyse intent, register and audience. In consecutive mode they take notes with symbols; in simultaneous mode they work in booths, listening and speaking at the same time (décalage). They manage honorifics (tú, usted, don/doña), humour and emotion, and ask for clarification when meaning is unclear in high-stakes settings such as courts and hospitals. Ethics demand accuracy and impartiality.
stages.mnemonic: Interpretar el sentido, no solo las palabras.
items: a sign of respect, like don
sentences: We will think about it, he said.
Respect is shown through the pronoun.

gq.q: In "Ya veremos", a speaker might intend...
o: a definite yes, said in a very polite way
gq.why: The phrase is often a vague deferral.

o: The short delay between speaker and interpreter
A type of dictionary that interpreters use in the booth
gq.why: The interpreter lags a few seconds to understand before speaking.

panel.q: Why should an interpreter ask for clarification in a court?
o: An error could change the legal outcome
panel.why: Accuracy is paramount where decisions have serious effects.

panel.q: How can a literal interpretation of politeness formulas mislead?
panel.model: A polite formula may mean something different from its words, such as a refusal, so the interpreter must convey the intent and tone.
panel.why: Pragmatic equivalence.

panel.q: Which is a risk of rendering a polite refusal as a plain "No"?
o: It may damage the relationship by changing the tone
It is always more accurate and it saves time for everyone
panel.why: Interpreters convey meaning and force, not only words.

teach.model: Speakers often mean more than they say. A polite phrase can be a refusal. An interpreter listens for intent, tone and cultural meaning, and asks for clarification when an error could be costly.

points.ask: What else should I listen for?

stages.title: Language variation and dialectology
stages.hook: Is the Spanish of Buenos Aires, Mexico City, Bogotá and Madrid one language or several? Dialectologists have an answer.
explain: Dialectology maps variation in pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar. Spanish is a pluricentric language with norms in several regions. Features: seseo (c and z as /s/) in Latin America, Andalusia and the Canaries; distinción in northern and central Spain; aspiration or loss of final s in the Caribbean, Andalusia and Chile; yeísmo (ll and y merged) widespread, with sheísmo in the River Plate; voseo in Argentina, Uruguay, Central America and parts of Colombia and Chile; leísmo, laísmo and loísmo in parts of Spain; ustedes replacing vosotros in the Americas and the Canaries.

Contact with Quechua, Guaraní, Nahuatl, Mayan languages, Catalan, Galician and Basque, and with English in the US, shapes local Spanish. Spanglish and code-switching are natural in bilingual communities. The Academy network (ASALE) accepts several norms. Prejudice about accents is social, not linguistic.
items: c and z pronounced as s

gq.q: Which feature is typical of most of Latin America?
gq.why: Latin America generally has seseo and ustedes.

o: It has several accepted standard norms
It is only spoken in Spain
gq.why: There are respected norms in Spain and in several American countries.

panel.q: Why is one accent not linguistically superior?
o: Some accents have no grammar of their own
panel.why: All varieties are rule-governed.

panel.q: Why do bilingual communities code-switch?
panel.model: Code-switching is a natural resource that expresses identity and adapts to topic, audience and situation.
panel.why: Sociolinguistic function.

panel.q: Which language contributed Spanish words like "papa" and "cóndor"?
panel.why: Quechua gave papa, cóndor and many other words.

teach.model: Spanish has many regional varieties with different sounds, words and grammar. Several countries have their own norms. Contact with other languages shapes them. All varieties follow rules, and none is worse.

stages.title: Specialised scientific or technical language
stages.hook: Why does a medical report say "El paciente presenta fiebre" and not "El paciente tiene mucha calentura"?
explain: Scientific and technical Spanish relies on Greek and Latin roots (cardiología, hipertensión, termodinámica), precise definitions, nominal phrases and the impersonal "se": "Se calentó la muestra a 80 °C". Units follow the SI, with a space between the number and the unit, and decimal comma or point depending on the country. Abbreviations and acronyms are common (ADN, OMS), and many anglicisms enter science ("software", "chip").

The structure of research follows IMRyD (Introducción, Métodos, Resultados y Discusión). Technical manuals use imperatives or infinitives and consistent terms: "Desconecte el aparato antes de limpiarlo". Define technical terms on first use. Avoid unnecessary anglicisms when a standard Spanish term exists, e.g. "ratón" for mouse (computing) and "cortafuegos" for firewall.
sentences: The sample was heated to eighty degrees.
The patient presents with a fever.

gq.q: What does ADN stand for in Spanish?
gq.why: ADN is the Spanish form of DNA.

gq.q: Which structure organises a scientific paper?

panel.q: Why is the impersonal "se" common in methods sections?
o: The action matters more than who did it
Spanish has no active voice in scientific writing
panel.why: Focus on procedure and objectivity.

panel.q: Why is consistent terminology crucial in technical manuals?
panel.model: Using the same term for the same thing avoids confusion and mistakes, which matters especially for safety instructions.
panel.why: Precision and safety.

panel.q: Which Spanish term replaces the anglicism "firewall"?
panel.why: Cortafuegos is the recommended Spanish term.

teach.model: Scientific Spanish is precise and often impersonal. Papers follow introduction, methods, results and discussion. Many terms come from Greek and Latin. Manuals use clear commands and the same term every time.

stages.title: Integrated proficiency project
stages.hook: Can you combine sounds, grammar, register and culture in one real Spanish project?
explain: The integrated project combines research, reading, discussion, writing and speaking. A sample task: investigate how a word or expression differs across Spanish-speaking countries, then report findings in a short article and a five-minute presentation. Steps: formulate a research question, gather examples from reliable sources, compare and categorise them, draw cautious conclusions, and cite sources.

Evaluate your level with the CEFR (Marco común europeo de referencia para las lenguas), A1 to C2, or with DELE diplomas from the Instituto Cervantes. At C1-C2 you handle complex texts, express ideas fluently, and adjust register and variety. Reflect: which structures are secure, which errors persist, and what will you practise next?
sentences: I collected examples from four countries.
Next I will practise the subjunctive.

o: Official diplomas of Spanish as a foreign language
A dictionary of Spanish words published by the Academy
gq.why: DELE diplomas are issued by the Instituto Cervantes.

gq.q: What should come first in a research project?
gq.why: The question guides data collection and analysis.

panel.q: A learner finds two examples of a word and states a rule for all Spanish. What is the error?
o: Using the passive voice too often in a report
panel.why: Conclusions must match the quantity and range of evidence.

panel.q: Why is self-assessment useful for a language learner?
panel.model: It shows progress, strengths and persistent errors, so that you can set goals and plan practice.
panel.why: Metacognition.

panel.q: Which output best combines reading, writing and speaking?
o: A researched article plus a short presentation
A long vocabulary list with translations in the margin
panel.why: An integrated task uses several skills for a real purpose.

teach.model: A project uses all your skills. Start with a question, collect examples from several places, compare them and report cautiously. Then reflect on your progress and plan what to practise next.
